name: Surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE)

lead: SARPE widens the upper jaw in adults whose palate suture has fused, giving a broader upper arch, roomier bite and, as forum posters hope, a fuller, better-proportioned midface and smile.

A surgeon makes bone cuts to release the maxilla, then an expander is turned gradually while new bone fills the gap. It is a recognized treatment for transverse maxillary deficiency, a narrow upper jaw that can cause crossbite and crowding. Clinical literature reports dental and skeletal outcomes rather than facial appearance.

paras: It is planned with an orthodontist, done under general anaesthesia, and the expander is turned daily for a few weeks, followed by months of retention and usually braces. Alternatives such as miniscrew-assisted expansion (MARPE) have been developed for some adults.
Reviews catalogue complications. Common effects include discomfort, swelling and a gap between the front teeth. The procedure involves general anaesthesia and bone cuts, with recovery restrictions.

web.title: Surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE) — Grokipedia

angle.text: Adults who want a wider upper jaw use SARPE when non-surgical expansion is no longer an option, and forum posters link the widening to a fuller, better-proportioned face. Skeletal widening is established for narrow-jaw bite problems; its facial-appearance effects are mostly reported anecdotally.

lead: Surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE), also called SARME, is a combined surgical and orthodontic procedure that widens the upper jaw in people whose midpalatal suture has fused after puberty. A surgeon makes bone cuts to release resistance, after which an expander appliance is gradually activated to widen the maxilla.[1][2][3]

It is a recognized treatment for transverse maxillary deficiency, a narrow upper jaw relative to the lower, which can cause posterior crossbite and crowding.[1][2] In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as an option for widening the upper jaw and face in adults when non-surgical expansion is considered no longer effective.[4]
Non-surgical alternatives, such as miniscrew-assisted expansion (MARPE), have been developed to avoid surgery in some adult patients.[5][6]

paras: In growing children and adolescents, tooth-borne expanders can separate the midpalatal suture, but expansion in adults is slower and more uncomfortable and often becomes mostly dental.[2][3] SARPE adds osteotomies to release the bony resistances around the maxilla before expansion.[1][2]

Grokipedia describes the surgeon's cuts, placement of a cemented expander such as a Hyrax, activation of about half a millimetre per day over several weeks, and retention of the device for four to six months while new bone forms.[1] The Wikipedia article on palatal expansion describes SARPE as an oral and maxillofacial surgeon cutting the midpalatal suture and inserting the expander, which the orthodontist then attaches to the upper molars.[3]

Palatal expansion was first described by Emerson Angell in 1860, and the Hyrax expander was introduced in 1968.[3] Grokipedia traces surgical assistance through corticotomies proposed by H. Kole in 1959, osteotomies described in 1969 and 1972, and standardized SARPE techniques in the 1980s.[1] An outpatient SARPE technique with long-term stability was reported in 1992, and bone-borne transpalatal distraction was described in 1999 to avoid drawbacks of tooth-borne devices.[7][8]

A literature review in 2008 summarized SARPE as having gradually gained popularity for correcting transverse deficiency in skeletally mature patients, where correction is more challenging than in young patients.[9] A study reported skeletal and dental changes following SARPE.[2] Grokipedia states that studies report relapse of roughly 5 to 25 percent, compared with higher rates for non-surgical expansion in older adolescents.[1]

Claims about facial appearance effects, such as widening of the midface, are discussed in forums; the clinical literature located here concerns dental and skeletal outcomes and nasal and bite function rather than aesthetics ratings.

A literature review and case report catalogued complications of SARPE.[10] Grokipedia lists temporary discomfort, swelling and a gap between the upper front teeth as common side effects.[1] Bone-borne distraction was developed partly to address anchorage loss, relapse, cortical fenestration and buccal root resorption seen with tooth-borne devices.[8]

A miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion method was devised so that some patients could avoid a two-stage surgical approach and its periodontal effects and relapse.[5] A later report described non-surgical treatment of transverse deficiency in adults using microimplant-assisted expansion.[6] Wikipedia notes MARPE is less invasive than SARPE and produces more skeletal expansion than tooth-based methods.[3]

A looksmax.org thread presents SARPE as simpler and better designed for people past puberty than mewing or mid-palatal suture-based approaches, arguing that the maxilla acts as a hinge for other facial bones.[4] A reply in the thread quotes a cost for orthognathic surgery in Spain starting around 15,000 euros and up to 40,000 euros in complex cases, noting it is often considered cosmetic and not insured.[4]

Clinical research includes reviews and cohort studies of skeletal and dental changes and complications.[9][2][10] Registered randomized trials include a three-segment versus two-segment technique trial (50 patients), a comparison of two SARME techniques (20 patients), a trial comparing segmental Le Fort I with SARME (90 patients), and tooth-borne versus hybrid expanders (32 patients, not yet recruiting).[11][12][13][14]

lore.intro: SARPE is discussed on looksmax.org as an adult route to a wider maxilla when other expansion options are considered unavailable.[4]

claims.claim: SARPE widens the maxilla in adults, which also widens and improves the face.
Non-surgical methods such as mewing or MSE stop working after adolescence or about age 25.
The procedure is expensive and may be classed as cosmetic.

timeline.event: Emerson Angell publishes the first paper on palatal expansion.[3]
Kole proposes selective corticotomies to reduce bony resistance.[1]
Biederman introduces the tooth-borne Hyrax expander.[3]
Outpatient SARPE technique with long-term stability reported.[7]
Miniscrew-assisted nonsurgical palatal expansion reported as an alternative.[5]
